notes.meaning: Habakkuk begins a musical prayer to the Lord. The term used in the title points to a lively, emotional song with shifting rhythms. Even though difficult days are coming, the prophet turns his worries into worship on behalf of God's people.

Habakkuk responds with deep awe to the message God gave him about the coming judgment. He asks God to keep His saving work alive during these difficult years of hardship and captivity. He knows the people deserve punishment, so he asks God to show mercy in the middle of His anger.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An older reading of the Greek translation rendered this phrase as being known between two living creatures, which early Christian writers applied to Jesus lying between two animals in the manger.

notes.meaning: The prophet looks back to how God revealed His holy presence from the southern wilderness lands near Mount Sinai. The skies shone with His bright majesty, and the whole earth was moved to praise Him. Remembering how God appeared to save His people in the past gives believers strong hope for the future.

God's appearance is described as blazing like the brightest sunlight. Beams of light flash like rays from His hand, showing His mighty strength. Yet even this blinding brilliance is only a veil that hides how truly great His full power is.

Terrible plagues and burning sickness march ahead of God and follow in His footsteps. These deadly forces serve as His servants, ready to carry out His commands against the enemies of His people. This shows that the Lord rules over all sickness and uses His power to defend His own.

The Lord pauses to look over the land and divide it among the tribes, making the nations shake in fear. Even the oldest mountains and hills crumble before His presence. God has always acted with this same unchanging, eternal power to protect His people.

Nearby desert nations, like Cushan and Midian, are gripped with terror as God leads His people forward. Their tent curtains tremble because they see what the Almighty can do. Hearing what God has done to save His servants makes even strong enemies lose heart.

Habakkuk asks if the Lord was angry with the rivers and the sea when He split them apart. The answer is no; God altered nature because He was riding out like a warrior on chariots to bring salvation to His people. All of creation obeys the Lord when He moves to rescue those who belong to Him.

God draws His war bow out of its case, ready to fight according to the promises He swore to the tribes of Israel. He also breaks open the dry ground so that fresh streams of water can gush out. God always keeps His word, even when it takes a miracle to provide for His flock.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Splitting the earth with rivers is likely poetic imagery describing intense thunderstorms that trigger rushing flash floods, rather than an earthquake cracking the ground.

notes.meaning: The mountains shake when they see God, and violent waters sweep across the land. The deep sea roars and lifts up its towering waves like hands raised in obedience to its Maker. Nothing in nature can block the path when God decides to deliver His people.

The sun and moon halt in the sky, just as they did in the days of Joshua. They pause while God sends out lightning and weapons like arrows to fight for Israel. Even the heavenly lights yield to the greater glory of God's power.

The Lord marches through the earth in righteous anger to judge the wicked. He crushes evil nations underfoot the way oxen trample wheat on a threshing floor. God will not allow wicked rulers to torment His people forever.

God went into battle to deliver His chosen nation and the leader He had set apart. He struck down the head of the wicked enemy and tore down their evil house from top to bottom. God completely overthrows the strongholds of evil to keep His people safe.

differ.view: The phrase refers directly to Christ the Messiah, through whom God accomplished all historical deliverances and ultimately conquered Satan.
The anointed refers to the entire consecrated people of Israel whom God set apart and saved as a whole nation.
The anointed refers to the historical leaders God chose to guide Israel, such as Moses, Joshua, and King David.

notes.meaning: The enemy rushed in like a fierce storm, eager to destroy the helpless Israelites in secret. Instead, God turned their own weapons back on them, piercing their leaders with their own spears. God often brings down proud oppressors by using their own evil schemes against them.

God led His people straight through the surging waters of the Red Sea as if riding on war horses. He created a dry highway through deep floods where no human path existed. No obstacle is too deep or wide for the Lord to guide His children through.

Hearing about the coming Babylonian invasion shakes Habakkuk to his core, making his lips quiver and his body feel weak. Yet he resolves to wait quietly for the day of trouble to fall upon the invaders. Holy fear of God's word teaches the believer how to find quiet trust during hard times.

The prophet pictures the total loss of all food and livelihood, with bare fruit trees, ruined harvests, and empty animal pens. Even if every earthly comfort is wiped out, he chooses to celebrate and take joy in the Lord who saves him. True faith does not depend on full storehouses, because God Himself is the believer's greatest treasure.

Habakkuk finds his true strength in God the Lord, who gives him sure-footed steps like a deer bounding over rocky heights. The closing note directs the temple choir to sing this psalm with stringed instruments. God gives believers the ability to rise above danger and walk with joy through the hardest places.
